q: Cross into Germany and the same black grape is called Lemberger; cross into Hungary and it is Kekfrankos. Sour cherry, peppery spice, high acid and real tannic grip. What does Austria call it?
exp: Blaufrankisch is the serious red of Burgenland and the one that changes most from soil to soil, lean on the iron slate of the far south and broad on Mittelburgenland clay. It is also one of Zweigelt's two parents.

q: Dark cherry, a silky texture, and a name taken from the saint's day in mid-August when the berries begin to colour. Which Austrian red?
exp: Sankt Laurent has long been thought a relative of Pinot Noir and behaves like one: thin skins, early ripening and a habit of setting fruit unevenly. The Thermenregion around Tattendorf and the northern shore of the Neusiedler See are its heartlands.

q: Deep heavy clay in a strip of Burgenland along the Hungarian border grows so much of one variety that the district is nicknamed after it. Which district?
exp: Growers call it Blaufrankischland, and Horitschon, Deutschkreutz and Neckenmarkt are its villages. The clay holds water and yields a fuller, darker, riper Blaufrankisch than the thinner soils further south.

q: Iron in the soil gave one southern Burgenland district its name, and it turns out the leanest, most peppery Blaufrankisch in the country. Which?
exp: Eisen is iron, and the slate there is stained rusty with it. The wines are lighter in body and higher in acid than Mittelburgenland's, which is the clearest demonstration Austria offers that this grape reads its site.

q: Limestone and mica schist on a range of hills west of the Neusiedler See carry a DAC covering both whites and a red off the same ground. Which?
exp: The Leithagebirge separates the lake from the Vienna basin, and its DAC takes Gruner Veltliner, Weissburgunder, Chardonnay and Neuburger for white and Blaufrankisch for red. Rust sits at the southern end of the same shore with a DAC of its own for sweet wine.

q: A lake on the Hungarian border spreads across a huge area yet averages barely a metre in depth, ringed by a wide belt of reeds. What does it do for the wines grown around it?
opts: It supplies the irrigation the sandy eastern shore depends on
It reflects enough light to ripen Cabernet Sauvignon fully
It cools the vineyards enough to hold the harvest back to December
It raises autumn humidity, so noble rot takes hold
exp: The Neusiedler See is a steppe lake with no real outflow, and reeds cover about half of it. Warm shallow water and reed beds put moisture and morning mist into the autumn air, and Botrytis cinerea takes hold in the vineyards on the eastern shore in nearly every vintage.

q: Sandy flats on the eastern side of the lake are dotted with shallow salt ponds and hold the villages of Illmitz and Apetlon. What is that corner called?
exp: Seewinkel means the corner of the lake, and its water table sits so close to the surface that mist forms readily. It is among the most dependable places in Europe for botrytis-affected sweet wine, which is why the two villages are famous out of all proportion to their size.

q: Morning fog burns off into warm dry afternoons through October beside the lake. Why does a sweet-wine grower need that alternation rather than damp alone?
opts: The alternation kills the wild yeast, so fermentation can be controlled
The fog freezes the water in the berry and the afternoon thaws the sugar out
The damp lets noble rot take hold, and dry warmth stops grey rot
The damp swells the berries and the dry afternoons then split them open
exp: Botrytis needs moisture to infect and dryness to concentrate; unbroken wet turns the same fungus into grey rot, which ruins the crop. Water evaporates through the punctured skin, so sugar, acid and flavour all climb together.

q: Storks nest on the chimneys of a small free city on the western shore of the lake, and its name attaches to a historic sweet wine. Which town?
exp: Rust bought its standing as a free city in 1681, reputedly with a payment partly in wine, and has guarded the Ausbruch name ever since. Illmitz and Gols lie on the far shore and Eisenstadt is the provincial capital inland.

q: Shrivelled botrytis berries are often too dry to yield anything under the press. What did the traditional Ruster method add to get them moving?
opts: Sugar syrup made from concentrated must, added at the press
Neutral grape spirit poured over them, as in a fortified wine
Fresh must or wine from healthy grapes of the same vineyard
Water heated enough to dissolve the sugar out of the skins
exp: Ausbruch sits between Beerenauslese and Trockenbeerenauslese on the Austrian must-weight ladder, and its name comes from breaking the shrivelled berries out of the bunch. The historic definition allowed only must or wine off the same vineyard and the same harvest, which is what kept the practice from being plain dilution. Rust's own designation no longer allows the addition at all, so the modern wine is pressed from the dried fruit alone.

q: Bunches are laid out on reed mats or straw and left to dry for months before they see a press. Which Austrian Pradikat does that produce?
exp: Stroh is straw and Schilf is reed, so the same Pradikat answers to Strohwein or Schilfwein, and the lake shore has no shortage of reeds. The law requires the fruit to rest on straw or reeds until it reaches the necessary must weight, generally three months or more, and the concentration comes from plain evaporation rather than from any fungus.

q: Steep green hills on the Slovenian border grow the Sauvignon Blanc that made Styria's reputation. Which region?
exp: Southern Styria works slopes so sharp they are farmed more like Alpine meadows than vineyards, and Sauvignon Blanc and Morillon are its calling cards. The Vulkanland to the east sits on extinct volcanoes and leans to Traminer, while Weststeiermark is Schilcher country.

q: A ferociously tart pink wine pressed from Blauer Wildbacher is the speciality of western Styria. What is it called?
exp: Schilcher is bracing enough to divide a room and is drunk locally almost to the exclusion of anything else. Sturm is part-fermented must sold in autumn, Uhudler is a curiosity of southern Burgenland made from hybrid vines, and Bergwein means wine off slopes steeper than twenty-six percent.

q: Several white varieties share one Viennese vineyard, are picked on the same day and go into the vat together. What must be true of the mix for the city's DAC?
opts: At least five varieties, all of them indigenous to Austria
At least three varieties, with the largest no more than half
Any number of varieties, provided each is fermented separately first
Exactly three varieties in equal proportion
exp: Wiener Gemischter Satz is a field blend, interplanted and co-fermented, which is a different animal from a cuvee assembled after the fact. The third variety has to reach at least a tenth of the blend, so the rule bites at both ends. Vienna is the only major capital still farming serious commercial vineyard inside its own boundary.

q: A bunch of pine branches hangs over a doorway on the edge of Vienna and the grower inside is pouring his own wine by the jug. What is the establishment called?
exp: The branch means ausg'steckt, hung out, and signals that this grower is open now; the right to sell one's own wine on the premises rests on an imperial decree of 1784. Heuriger is also the wine itself, meaning this year's, and it keeps the name until Saint Martin's Day the following November.

q: Austrian sparkling wine of protected origin climbs three steps, each demanding more of the grower than the last. What are they, from the bottom up?
opts: Sekt Austria Klassik, Sekt Austria Reserve, Sekt Austria Prestige
Sekt Austria, Sekt Austria Reserve, Sekt Austria Grosse Reserve
exp: Each step tightens origin, method and time on the lees together, so the pyramid is a single ladder rather than three separate rules; the entry tier was called Klassik until the rebranding to Sekt Austria in 2022 and now carries no qualifier at all. Gebietswein, Ortswein and Riedenwein is the still-wine DAC pyramid, and Steinfeder, Federspiel and Smaragd belongs to the Wachau; neither has anything to do with sparkling wine.
